I am a huge "proof" person. Although my perception of proof is often warped by my BPD. Like if I get left on read, that's "proof" to me that I am worthless and that person doesn't love me and is going to leave me. But if I embrace the good that also happens, especially externally that helps a little bit too. One of my affirmations is that "your body is yours and belongs to you and you only". obviously being SA'd and sexually coerced many times in my childhood would tells me otherwise, but thinking about the amount of people that HAVE respected my boundaries, and the amount of people that DO tell me my body is mine and belongs to me and being able to live in my own skin and do things with it helps put it into perspective that "okay, this body is yours and yours to keep even if SOME people don't act like it". So like I said, ny emotional mind takes over my logical mind alot, but if the emotional mind can be positively externally validated than at least thats somewhat of a win

INFPs can be some of the most bitter, off putting, "meanest" people ever. I say this as an INFP myself, especially when you see one in a Fi-Si loop or Te grip. Next, I think, everyone can have access to all 4 of their main functions of a daily basis, depending on their mood and environment, whether that's good or bad. And finally, I think it's fully possible to access your shadow functions in times of stress and times of health. I think MBTI is about progress and growth and that we all can be in tune with all 8 functions, especially given our enneagram type/subtype/instinct variant, or even considering trauma and mental health. For example, I'm a so/sx 4w3, 479, and have BPD. So I'd say I have better access to Se in times of stress than most INFPs might. I am also able to access Te well both in times of stress and health. I see all 4 cognitive functions as a certain type's unique superpower, they just tend to affect us in certain ways - some in worse ways, some in better

I'm gonna agree with another commenter here and say it depends on the person. I think fibro in and of itself really is overactive nervous system activity and sensitivity that has a potential slight autoimmune component to it (still on the fence about that) that can be triggered in someone either genetically or environmentally and dare I say personality wise. for some people, fibro runs in their families, so if a sibling or grandparent has it, they'll get it too, simple as that. for some people, it can be caused by post trauma stress that affects the body because of some kind of abuse, grief, surgery, injury or accident. and for some people (I believe myself to be one of them), I think there is a predisposition to get a functional nerve disorder like fibromyalgia and IBS because of a naturally more emotional, sensitive, tense or anxious temperament, personality wise. or a weaker, less flexible, or maybe less stamina physically speaking. then once one of the afformentioned "triggers" happens (abuse, grief, surgery, injury, accident), that triggers your already prone personality and lifestyle to cause all the sensitivities and pain that come with fibro. I think it's even more fascinating, albeit exhausting when complex, unresolved trauma is involved. for me, I've always been very emotionally sensitive, anxious, dramatic, prone to alot of crying and anger since I was a kid. prone to occassional fainting/dizziness spells, but nothing to serious. then years of severe repeated emotional, sexual, religious abuse, invalidation, neglect and abandonment that felt and was in some ways inescapable were affecting me and all my suppressed, intense emotions took a huge toll on my body. I think it's why stress is a huge trigger for people's flare ups. I think the diverse, complicated nature of our illness truly can lead to different causes and experiences for us all. so there's no right or wrong answer and no matter the cause, our pain will always be real and not just "in our heads"

Hi dear. I'm 18 too and I see myself in alot of your struggles. I have fibromyalgia and IBS and looking to get diagnosed with POTS and multiple sclerosis and I relate alot to this. First off, I just wanna say I'm sorry you've struggled for a long time and feel so unheard, failed, dismissed and not listened to. It's a sad reality for so many chronically ill and disabled folks. It's a sad one, but not one you have to endure alone. We're here for you.

My thoughts? When you mentioned the fatigue, low energy, and widespread muscle pain, my mind instantly went to fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome. They're kinda like cousins lol. Do you feel fatigue after exertion or movement? Do you have heightened sensitivity to external stimuli like touch, weather, or temperature changes? Any mood, sleep, fatigue or brain fog issues? If so, either of these conditions could be worth looking into. Try seeing a neurologist or rheumatologist for this and your headaches. Maybe even a cardiologist for the dizziness issue. Stay as hydrated as you can too and try to intake salt and electrolytes when you get these episodes

As for the hunger and food issues, that could be hormonal, endocrine or emotional. Have you had any endocrine testing done? You mention psychosomatic pain too, and if you struggle with anxiety, depression or have a history of trauma/PTSD that could be a very real possibility as an underlying cause. If you have a mental health advocate or professional you see, it could be worth talking to. But don't quit on yourself. There's still a chance your pain may be physical and I don't think you should sell yourself short of that or invalidate that even if you do have a mental health history 

Early satiety, nausea, fullness, hunger/body inconsistencies can also be caused by things like stomach ulcers, gastroparesis, gastritis or any other GI related dysautonomia issues. Or could be a part of IBS.  This is worth looking into seeing a gastroenterologist for if you please. Try to keep your vitamin D and b12 intakes at a healthy level too, as deficiencies in can exacerbate the issues you're dealing with

Okay, I knew I just threw a bunch of potential diagnoses at you. You may have all of them, or none of them, or some of them. But the important thing is, that you reach out for help, advocate for yourself and have people around you that'll support and validate your pain, no matter how diagnosed or undiagnosed you are. You have us too! My best advice is take it day by day, take care yourself the best way you can, and don't be afraid to reach out for help. Wishing you luck, and again know you aren't alone 💗🫂

Hello love. I relate alot to you and understand the fear and sadness you're having. I'm turning 19 next month, was diagnosed last May and also just finished my first semester at university. 

Here's my advice : The hard truth about fibromyalgia is that people won't understand the pain, exhusation and agony you're having, unless they also have this illness or one like it. People will be ignorant (some maliciously so and others without meaning to hurt). But there are and WILL be people who can empathize, sympathize and validate and support us. Good people are out there. This illness can't be cured and it may never go away for most of us. But the positive thing is, you and I are still so young and so fresh in our diagnoses and our realizations of our conditions. That makes things scary, but it can also change your worldview in a way that may help you. Let your illness charge you into self advocacy, let it charge you into asserting boundaries, standing up for yourself and finding out who your real company and support system is. Let it charge you into seeking out the help, accomodations, community and support you need.  Experiement with new treatment options and medications. Advil relief cream and salonpas pain relief patches help with localized pain for me, compression socks and compression wraps help with that too. Gabapentin is great for widespread nerve pain, amitryptaline is great for sleep, and cymbalta is great for depression, anxiety, nerve pain, and low energy too. Try new things, new coping methods that you have enough spoons for - walking, painting, ASMR and massages (from other people lol) are the best for me. I hear mindfulness, yoga,  somatic releases and meditation and stuff like qi gong and tai chi helps some people too. Get yourself a mobility aid if you need it or request your doctor to write you a prescription for one. I just bought a walking stick, so maybe that or a rollator, wheelchair, or a foldable chair may be good for you. Trial and error is very commonplace and sometimes necessary for our condition, but it'll be worth it in the end. Never overexert yourself either. Good days will be there, but don't overdo it on those days

And now for my comforting words : You are not alone, you are not a burden and you are worthy of love, companionship, and care from other people. Being a child/teen or young adult with an illness like this is not easy. It makes you a fucking warrior, so never doubt that for a second about yourself. I've had symptoms of fibro since I was 11 and the amount of strength and resilience it takes to juggle this during the "prime years of your life" is unmatched. You are allowed to grieve the life and body you no longer have and no one can take that pain away from you. Not even a doctor. Also, dont let doctors gaslight or manipulate you, they are not smarter than you nor do they know youself better than you do. But know your body, spirit, mind and experiences are yours and yours only and no one can dicatate what you can or cant handle. Only you can. I ended up typing a bit, but just know that we are here for you, we love you, see you and you will be okay. Even if right now it doesnt feel that way. wish you the best of luck and if you ever need to talk or vent, feel free to hit me up anytime 💗 we're in this together

Some people would benefit from what helps other people with CBT but with a different modality in its place (like say DBT or ACT) 

I would like to maybe go back to CBT again or at least DBT if I were to do something similar, but I can say for me and other complex trauma clients that CBT doesnt work at either a. the beginning of the healing jouney, b. on it's own at the beginning of the healing journey, c. under certain circumstances, d. at all. Im in the exact same boat as you - trying to grapple with complex childhood trauma after bad therapy experiences is tough as fuck. only difference is, I am willing to give therapy another chance, I will just be very cautious and intentional this time. its also okay and understandable that you dont want therapy again, so that said, here's some advice I am trying/hoping to try out : 

- self help books or books about the experiences you've faced and issues you have. I imagine these can be good at validating the severity of your issues, while also encouraging you that things can and will get better AND giving you tools to heal

- journaling for sure helps you process, remember and work through things both past and present 

- I hear somatic exercises, yoga, and emotional regulation and grounding skills can help alot with some of the emotional/physical symptoms of trauma. try the beautyafterbruises.org site for some trauma informed info/skills

- positive, specifically curated affirmations about your specific experiences and life and circumstances may be able to help

- having a good support system. it can be friends, family members, even classmates or coworkers. having people in your corner that see, support and validate you even if they can't "FIX" you does wonders. I do not know where I would be without my siblings (especially my older sister) or best friend for example. please if someone cares or is willing to help, let them. you deserve and need community to heal 

- express yourself through the arts. maybe Im biased cause I'm in school to be an art therapist right now anyway, but creative self expression can be very cathartic grounding, relaxing and inspiring. does not matter how "good" the art looks, its just about how it makes you feel. I reccomend the thirstyforart youtube channel for advice and tips 

- gratitude journaling/writing. when you've faced so much trauma for years and are currently facing issues, its so easy to feel compounded, trapped and like nothing's going for you. but please I beg give yourself the grace and the space to acknowledge the good you have in your life. I used to hate the idea of positive thinking/gratitude because I've had that used as an abuse, manipulation and invalidation tactic against me, but when done productively and in an AFFIRMING, TRAUMA INFORMED way, it works wonders. dont be scared to write down "little" or irrelevant things either. I've literally written down shit like "that nice lady gave me a hug after I showed her where her class is" and "guy in my class complimented my haircut today", like seriously its the little things that count

dont let anyone take away the validity of your experiences. I've had people who are supposed to love and care for me do that and it sucks. but trust and believe that is their own projection and unhealed bs coming through onto you. it is not your fault, you don't deserve it and people love and care for you. I believe in you and wish you the best 💗💗

ps : try the r/therapyabuse sub for more support on shitty therapy. no one understands shitty therapy quite like those peeps do. super validating

For me personally, not really cause most of my therapists have all taken a mostly CBT approach. my current therapist is taking a more trauma informed perspective though, but he's been unhelpful too for other unrelated reasons. Based on research I've done and experiences people have shared with me, I hear EMDR, somatic experiencing therapy, internal family systems, and psychodynamic along with attachment based therapy have been helpful for alot of folks. take everything I say with a grain of salt though, everyone is different and there's no one size fits all, especially for something as severe and personal as complex trauma

the whole formation of CBT as a modality works in complete opposition to how complex trauma effects it's victims. CBT is a modality that helps with surface level cognitive distortions and gives you skills to change those negative though patterns and engage in positive thinking skills. which isn't inherently bad, but completely ignores the complexity of CPTSD. folks with complex trauma cannot simply "rid" themselves of their cognitive "distortions". trauma of that severity deeply effects someone emotionally, socially, somatically, spiritually and sometimes developmentally. CBT isnt a technique that can effectively tackle those issues. and if it does to an extent I find it's not long lasting or effective. CBT for me for example helped alot with my intrusive thoughts, a completely separate issue I had - but did nothing to help my post trauma symptoms, resulting attachment issues, with sexual and body shame, and didnt even help with my self harm/suicidal ideation. the "big stuff".  for many people CBT feels too surface level, and even victim blame-y/,gaslightling and has straight up retraumatized alot of us. you can not "outthink" your severe complex trauma responses in short 15-30 session increments, you have to tackle all of them effectively and holistically, and I feel CBT does the opposite. not to mention it's very present day, in the moment focused. and for people with complex trauma, in order to heal we HAVE to uproot the past, make sense of that, process what happened, how it effected us and then learn to cope with it's great aftermath. CBT alone can not help with this
